_: The vocabulary. One entry per hack, and every number on screen is in here
with the study it came from. A hack with no `source` does not ship - the
brand is a health app, and a number nobody can chase is worth less than no
icon    a lucide name in icon-sources/package/icons/<name>.svg
clock   where it sits in the day. Drives the day bar and the row order
chips   what it costs the viewer. One is the shipped default: one chip
read at arm's length beats two chips read by nobody
metric  the caption under the dial - what changes
value   what the dial counts up to. Text, so '+250%' and '-2 H' both work
dir     up | down | time. The dial's colour, and nothing else
source  the citation. Prose, because it is read by a person, not parsed

morning light.source: Sharkey/Eastman, Sleep Med 2014-15: morning bright light on waking advanced sleep/wake timing and circadian phase markers by about 2 h. Also Leproult, JCEM 2001: dim->bright (150->4500 lux) in the early morning raises plasma cortisol within 15 min, which is the same clock being set.

cold finish.source: Sramek et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2000: immersion at 14 C raised plasma dopamine to 250% of baseline, rising gradually and staying up for hours with no crash after it. The 2 min chip is the shower-tail dose Huberman's synthesis settles on (1-3 min at 4-7 C), not the study's own hour.

walk after lunch.source: Sci Rep 2025 (s41598-025-07312-y): a 10 min walk taken immediately after glucose intake cut the peak from 181.9 to 164.3 mg/dL, p=0.028, d=0.73. That is -9.7%, rounded down. Self-selected pace, 3.8 km/h - a stroll, not a session.

last coffee.source: Caffeine's plasma half-life in healthy adults is about 5 h. Ten hours between the last cup and lights-out is two half-lives, so a quarter of the dose is left instead of the whole of it - 75% less than the same coffee taken at bedtime. Pure pharmacokinetics, no single trial: the number is arithmetic on a constant.

lights down.source: Phillips et al., PNAS 2019: evening room light suppresses melatonin, and the sensitivity spread is enormous - half the people tested lost 50% of their melatonin under less than 30 lux, which is dimmer than most living rooms. The dial states the benefit of dimming, which is the suppression not taken; the study measured the loss.

veg first.source: Shukla et al., Diabetes Care 2015;38:e98: the same meal eaten vegetables-and-protein-first rather than carbohydrate-first cut mean post-meal glucose by 28.6% at 30 min, 36.7% at 60 and 16.8% at 120, and the incremental AUC by 73%. Shukla 2019 (Diab Obes Metab) repeated it in prediabetes. -29% is the 30 min figure, the one a person would feel. The only entry in the table that costs nothing at all - it is an order, not a dose, which is why its chip reads 0 MIN.

7000 steps.source: Ding et al., Lancet Public Health 2025 (57 studies, 2014-2025, dose-response meta-analysis): 7000 steps a day against 2000 was associated with 47% lower all-cause mortality and 47% lower cardiovascular mortality. Observational, so association not cause, and the comparator matters - it is against 2000 steps, not against a person who already walks.

nose breathing.source: Balban et al., Cell Rep Med 2023 (Stanford): 5 min a day of cyclic sighing - long exhales - beat mindfulness meditation on both mood (p<0.05) and resting respiratory rate (p<0.05) over a month, and the people whose breathing slowed most were the ones whose mood rose most.

hydrate first.source: Ganio et al., Br J Nutr 2011 and Armstrong et al., J Nutr 2012: mild dehydration around 1-2% of body mass degrades vigilance, working memory and mood in both men and women. The +14% is the vigilance-error recovery reported in Ganio; treat it as directional, and prefer the plain claim - the deficit shows up long before thirst does.

stand up.source: Dunstan et al., Diabetes Care 2012: breaking 5 h of sitting with 2 min of light walking every 20 min cut the postprandial glucose incremental AUC by 24.1% against uninterrupted sitting. Restated here at the dose people will actually do - a few minutes an hour - so read it as the effect's size, not its exact schedule.

step outside.source: White et al., Scientific Reports 2019 (19 806 people, Monitor of Engagement with the Natural Environment): 120-179 min of nature contact in the past week against none gave OR 1.59 (95% CI 1.32-1.92) for reporting good health and 1.23 (1.08-1.40) for high wellbeing. There is a threshold - under 120 min showed no benefit at all - and it did not matter whether the time came in one visit or several. Cross-sectional, so association not cause.

no screens.source: Chang et al., PNAS 2015: reading on a light-emitting device before bed pushed melatonin onset later, cut evening sleepiness and lengthened the time taken to fall asleep by about 10 min against a printed book, over five nights.

last meal early.source: Gu et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2020: the same meal eaten at 22:00 rather than 18:00 left overnight glucose higher and fat oxidation lower in the same people. The magnitude is the study's own peak-glucose difference; the 3 h chip is the founder's own rule in CORE_STORY.md - last meal two or three hours before bed.

fibre first.source: Reynolds et al., Lancet 2019 (185 prospective studies, 58 trials, 135 million person-years): 25-29 g of dietary fibre a day against under 15 g was associated with 15-30% lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, and the dose-response curve was still falling at 35 g. -20% is the middle of that band. Observational for the mortality end, though the trials support the mechanism.

lift twice.source: Momma et al., Br J Sports Med 2022 (meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies): 30-60 min a week of muscle-strengthening activity was associated with 10-17% lower risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, total cancer and diabetes. The curve is J-shaped and flat past an hour - more is not better here, which is the unusual part and the reason the chip says 40 min a WEEK. Independent of aerobic activity; combined, the two are additive.

see people.source: Holt-Lunstad et al., PLoS Medicine 2010 (meta-analysis, 148 studies, 308 849 people, average 7.5 y follow-up): people with stronger social relationships had a 50% greater likelihood of survival, OR 1.50. The effect held across age, sex, health status and cause of death, and is comparable in size to quitting smoking. The only entry in this table whose dose is not a number, because the studies measure integration rather than minutes.

heat then cold.source: Laukkanen et al., JAMA Intern Med 2015 (Kuopio, 2315 men, 20 y): 2-3 sauna sessions a week associated with 27% lower cardiovascular mortality against once a week, and 4-7 a week with 50%. Observational, so association not cause - and the only entry here that is not free, which is why it is not in the shipped five.

move most days.source: Chekroud et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2018 (1.2 million US adults, CDC BRFSS 2011-2015): people who exercised reported 43.2% fewer days of poor mental health in the past month than people matched on age, sex, income, education and physical health who did not. The dose curve is U-shaped, which is the unusual part - 45 min three to five times a week was the optimum, and over 90 min a session, or more than 23 sessions a month, was worse than not exercising at all. Team sports, cycling and aerobic/gym were the strongest categories. Cross-sectional and self-reported, so association not cause.

brain dump.source: Scullin et al., J Exp Psychol Gen 2018;147(1):139-146 (57 adults, in-lab polysomnography): five minutes of writing out what still needs doing, immediately before lights out, put people to sleep in 16 min against 25 for those who wrote instead about what they had already finished - about 9 min sooner, measured on EEG rather than reported. The more specific the to-do list the faster they fell asleep, and the more specific the completed-tasks list the slower. One night and a small sample, which is why the chip is the dose and the dial is only the difference.

cycle to work.source: Celis-Morales et al., BMJ 2017;357:j1456 (UK Biobank, 263 450 commuters, 5 y median follow-up): cycling to work against a non-active commute was associated with 52% lower cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.48), 41% lower all-cause mortality and 40% lower cancer mortality. Walking to work showed the cardiovascular benefit only past about 10 km a week. The chip is the study population's own typical cycling load, roughly 30 miles a week; the benefit was dose-dependent, so half of it is not half the number. Observational, so association not cause - and cyclists differ from drivers in more than their commute.

take the stairs.source: Stamatakis et al., Atherosclerosis 2024 (meta-analysis, 9 cohort studies, 480 479 people): people who climbed stairs had 24% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.76) and 39% lower cardiovascular mortality than those who did not. The pooled comparison is stair-climbing against none rather than a dose, so the 5 FLOORS chip is the older cohort work's own threshold - Paffenbarger's Harvard alumni used about 35 flights a week - restated at what a person would actually count. Read the number as the effect's size, not as a prescription for five.

swap the soda.source: Malik et al., Diabetes Care 2010;33(11):2477-83 (meta-analysis, 8 prospective cohorts, 310 819 people): one to two sugar-sweetened drinks a day against less than one a month carried 26% greater risk of type 2 diabetes (RR 1.26) and 20% greater risk of metabolic syndrome. The dial states the risk not taken, which is the swap's side of the same number - the study measured the risk taken. Observational, and the drink is the exposure rather than the calories: the association held after adjusting for weight in most of the cohorts.

read a book.source: Bavishi, Slade & Levy, Soc Sci Med 2016;164:44-48 (Health and Retirement Study, 3 635 people over 50, 12 y): book readers had 20% lower mortality than non-readers (HR 0.80) and a survival advantage of 23 months - the +2 Y on the dial. Up to 3.5 h a week carried the benefit and more carried more, which is where the 30 MIN chip comes from. Books, not newspapers or magazines: periodical reading gave a much weaker effect, and the authors put it down to the deeper, slower kind of attention a book asks for. Observational, and reading is not randomly distributed.

eat slowly.source: Hurst & Fukuda, BMJ Open 2018;8:e019589 (59 717 Japanese adults with type 2 diabetes, insurance claims and annual checkups 2008-2013): against fast eaters, slow eaters were 42% less likely to be obese (OR 0.58) and normal-speed eaters 29% less likely, and slowing down was associated with falling BMI and waist circumference over the period. Eating speed was self-reported as fast, normal or slow, so the study has no dose - the 20 MIN chip is the time satiety signalling takes to arrive, which is the mechanism rather than this study's finding. Observational.

wash your hands.source: Aiello, Coulborn, Perez & Larson, Am J Public Health 2008;98(8):1372-81 (meta-analysis, 30 studies of hand hygiene in the community, not in hospitals): respiratory illness fell 21% and gastrointestinal illness 31%. The dial takes the SMALLER of the two, so it understates. Duration is the shaky part - the included trials range from plain soap-and-water education to alcohol gel and do not isolate a time, so 20 SEC is the public-health standard rather than any one study's dose. The effect is real and it is not large: this is the row that argues the poster's case by being modest.

sleep enough.source: Prather, Janicki-Deverts, Hall & Cohen, Sleep 2015;38(9):1353-9: 164 healthy adults wore wrist actigraphy for a week, were then quarantined, given rhinovirus in nasal drops and watched for five days. Sleeping under 6 h a night made them 4.2 times more likely to actually develop a cold than sleeping over 7 h; under 5 h, 4.5 times. Independent of age, BMI, season, stress, income, education and smoking. -76% is 1 - 1/4.2, the same finding stated from the well-slept side, because the dial reads the benefit and the study measured the cost. The exposure was deliberate and controlled, which makes this the best-designed study in this table.

more protein.source: Weigle et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2005;82(1):41-8 (19 adults, metabolic-ward controlled feeding then 12 weeks ad libitum): raising protein from 15% to 30% of energy while holding carbohydrate constant cut spontaneous calorie intake by 441 kcal a day - the subjects were not asked to eat less and did anyway - and they lost 4.9 kg, 3.7 kg of it fat. Small and short, and the mechanism is satiety rather than anything metabolic. The 30 G chip is a per-meal restatement of the study's whole-diet 30%: what a person can actually count.

water first.source: Dennis et al., Obesity 2010;18(2):300-7 (48 adults aged 55-75, randomised, 12 weeks on the same hypocaloric diet): the group told to drink 500 ml of water before every meal lost 7.0 kg against 5.3 kg - about 2 kg more, or 44% more weight off the same diet. Older adults only, and the effect is thought to be gastric distension, which empties faster in younger people. The dial reads the difference the water made, not the total lost.

cook at home.source: Mills et al., Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 2017;14:109 (11 396 UK adults, Fenland Study): eating home-cooked meals more than five times a week against less than three was associated with 24% lower likelihood of excess body fat and 28% lower likelihood of being overweight, plus more fruit and vegetables and better overall diet quality. Cross-sectional, so association not cause, and people who cook differ from people who do not in more than their cooking.

sleep window.source: Placeholder - has no defensible number and must not ship until it does. Kept as the shape of an entry, not as content.
